title: Understanding Post-Traumatic Headache: Causes, Symptoms, and Treatment
author: Power Of Patients
content:
Every year more than 1.5 million Americans suffer a traumatic brain injury (TBI). A TBI refers to a sudden injury that results in damage to the brain. It could result from a forceful blow to the head or from an object that pierces the skull.

A post-traumatic headache is closely associated with a TBI. Research indicates that a post-traumatic headache is a complication of a TBI in 30% to 90% of all cases.

If you or someone you love has recently experienced a post-traumatic headache, this blog post is for you. Here, we will take a closer look at the causes, symptoms, and treatment options. The latter includes Sallie from Power of Patients.

As noted in the introduction, TBIs and post-traumatic headaches can result from various types of head injuries. These include concussions, skull fractures, or any trauma that affects the head and neck area.

The reality today is that the exact cause of post-traumatic headaches is not fully understood. However, there are several factors that are believed to play a role. Let's explore some of these.

When a head trauma occurs, it can lead to damage to the brain tissue itself. The brain is a delicate organ, and any trauma can disrupt its normal functioning. This disruption can trigger a cascade of events that contribute to the development of headaches.

For example, inflammatory responses, chemical imbalances, ocular migraines, and altered blood flow within the brain can all contribute to the pain associated with post-traumatic headaches.

The head and neck region contains numerous nerves that are responsible for transmitting sensory information. During a head injury, these nerves can be stretched, compressed, or even damaged. This nerve dysfunction can lead to abnormal pain signaling, resulting in the development of headaches.

Another contributing factor is changes in blood flow within the brain and surrounding structures. Following a head injury, blood vessel changes can occur. These changes can indeed lead to altered blood flow patterns.

It is also worth highlighting the role of emotional and psychological factors. These factors can influence the development and perception of post-traumatic headaches.

Anxiety, depression, and stress can exacerbate pain symptoms. They can also make them feel more intense. The psychological impact of a traumatic event can contribute to the persistence and severity of post-traumatic headaches.

Note that the causes of post-traumatic headaches can vary from person to person. They may involve a combination of the above factors. Understanding the underlying causes can help to determine effective treatment plans in the long term.

Put simply, the main symptom of post-traumatic headache is pain. This pain can manifest itself in different ways. Generally, the pain resembles tension-type headaches or migraines.

 Symptoms can also vary in their duration and intensity. Let's explore some of the common symptoms associated with this condition.

The most prominent symptom is a persistent headache. The pain can range from mild to severe and may have different characteristics. For example, it is often described as:

Throbbing

Pressure-like

Dull

The location of the pain can vary as well. Some individuals may experience pain in specific areas of the head or behind the eyes.

Many people who experience post-traumatic headaches may have sensitivity to light (photophobia) and sound (phonophobia). For example, exposure to bright lights may exacerbate the headache symptoms. This can include sunlight or fluorescent lighting.

Similarly, loud noises or even normal ambient sounds may intensify the pain.

Post-traumatic headaches can be accompanied by feelings of nausea, and some individuals may experience vomiting as well. These symptoms can range from mild discomfort to severe bouts of nausea and frequent episodes of vomiting. Nausea and vomiting may worsen during periods of intense headaches.

1 in 4 American adults have some type of disability. The most common type of disability relates to cognition, with almost 13% of people experiencing serious difficulty with the following:

Concentrating

Remembering

Making decisions

Post-traumatic headaches can affect cognitive function. Individuals may find it challenging to focus on tasks, retain information, or perform mental activities that were previously effortless.

Post-traumatic headaches can often manifest with various vision disturbances. These can significantly impact an individual's daily life. These visual symptoms may include:

Blurred vision

Distorted vision

Sensitivity to bright      lights

Visual field defects

It's important to communicate any vision challenges to your healthcare provider. They can provide valuable information for diagnosis and treatment planning. There are also a number of strategies that can help alleviate vision-related symptoms, including:

Wearing sunglasses      outdoors

Reducing screen time

Modifying lighting      indoors

Using computer glasses

Addressing any vision challenges and seeking appropriate care can help manage post-traumatic headache symptoms and improve visual well-being.

Studies show that as many as 1 in 3 adults in the U.S. don't get enough sleep. This can have a major impact on our overall health and well-being. Post-traumatic headaches can also interfere with sleep patterns, which can result in difficulties:

Falling asleep

Staying asleep

Experiencing restful      sleep

Sleep disturbances can further contribute to overall fatigue and impact an individual's ability to cope with headache symptoms.

It is not uncommon for individuals with post-traumatic headaches to experience mood changes. These can include:

Irritability

Anxiety

Depression

The chronic nature of the headaches and their impact on daily life can take a toll on emotional well-being.

As with causes, it's important to note that symptoms can vary from person to person. Some individuals may experience a combination of these symptoms, while others may primarily have headaches with minimal associated symptoms. The intensity and frequency of the symptoms can also fluctuate over time.

The management of post-traumatic headaches involves a multidisciplinary approach. It should be tailored to the individual's specific symptoms and needs. Let's highlight some of the most common treatment options, including Sallie from Power of Patients.

After a head injury, it is crucial to allow the brain and body to rest and recover. This may involve taking time off work or reducing physical and cognitive activities that may exacerbate symptoms.

Over-the-counter pain relievers can help to relieve mild to moderate headaches. These include acetaminophen or ibuprofen. In more severe cases, prescription medications, including triptans or muscle relaxants, may be prescribed.

Making certain lifestyle changes can help manage post-traumatic headaches. These may include practicing stress-reduction techniques, such as:

Meditation

Deep breathing      exercises

Avoiding triggers (such      as caffeine and alcohol)

Maintaining a regular      sleep schedule

Proper hydration

Maintaining a healthy diet

Finding a supportive      environment

Regular exercise

Taking nutritional      supplements (i.e. Omega-3s)

It's essential to work closely with your healthcare provider to develop a comprehensive management plan.

For individuals with neck or head injuries, physical therapy may be beneficial. Therapists can provide exercises and techniques to improve neck and head movement, reduce muscle tension, and alleviate pain.

Undoubtedly, dealing with post-traumatic headaches can be challenging. It's not uncommon for individuals to seek support from a mental health professional, such as a psychologist or counselor. This can help individuals to cope with these challenges and develop strategies for managing their symptoms.
